body: A boy of fifteen is standing on a shingle bank with his coat over his arm, watching his father go backwards into a river nobody in their right mind would enter in March. There are perhaps thirty people on the bank and a dog that belongs to none of them. His father comes up, the water goes off him in sheets, and he makes a noise that is not a word. Before he has got his footing on the stones somebody at the back has started singing, and by the second line most of the bank has joined in, badly, in the wrong key, over the sound of the river. Nobody announced it and nobody was leading it. The boy is not singing, but he is not looking away either.

Something enormous had just happened to one person and the crowd around him did not applaud it, did not photograph it and did not discuss it. They sang. It is such a natural reaction that we barely notice how odd it is.

It is the oldest reaction there is. Israel walks out of the sea on dry ground, the water closes behind them, and the very next thing in the text is not a report, not a monument and not a law. It is a song, with a woman leading it and a tambourine in her hand.

It is worth staying with the sequence rather than admiring the picture, because the alternatives were all available. They could have built an altar of stones, and Israel builds plenty of those elsewhere. They could have written it down, appointed witnesses, set a feast day, held a council about what the sea meant. All of that comes later. But the first thing, before the ground was dry, was fifteen verses of poetry with a tune, and then Miriam takes a tambourine and the women go out after her with tambourines and dancing. Deliverance happens and the response is music, immediately, corporately, and with the whole body rather than only the mouth.

That instinct has a whole stretch of this dial given over to it. The band runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 of them on air today, and the largest single share of them are praise and worship frequencies. That proportion was a decision, not an accident of what was easy to make.

Building it that way costs something, because continuous praise is the hardest thing to keep honest over long hours. A teaching station can be true and quiet. A praise station that never stops is making a claim every three minutes, all night, into rooms where nothing whatever is happening — and it has to keep making it at four in the morning when almost nobody is listening. It is kept running anyway, because the alternative is a band that only celebrates when it has an audience, and that is not what Miriam was doing on the far bank with a river of water behind her.

The instinct has also quietly gone out of the culture, and out of a good deal of the church with it. Music has been demoted to the soft part of faith — the warm-up, the mood-setting, the twenty minutes before the serious content starts, with the serious content always being prose. Scripture does not treat song that way anywhere. It treats it as what people do when something has actually happened to them, which suggests that a generation which has stopped singing is telling on itself rather than on the music.

So the band is arranged with that at the front rather than the edges. The praise and worship formats sit together in the low three hundreds where a hand finds them without looking. The Hebraic and Messianic frequencies hold their own stretch, the international stations another, the children’s frequencies another again. Learn roughly where things sit and you can move about the dial by feel — which is precisely the skill a real band teaches and a search box never can.
Nothing here argues against writing things down. The question is what people reach for first.

Be fair to the report, because Exodus contains one and we would have nothing without it. Written testimony is checkable. It can be handed to somebody who was not there, examined by somebody who does not believe it, and corrected where it is wrong. A song can do none of that reliably. But a report is a thing you consult, and a consultation requires that you already know you want it. Nobody consults a document while driving to work. Nobody has a monument going in the kitchen. The report waits to be opened, and most of the hours of a human life are hours in which nobody is opening anything.
The sea closes, and somebody reaches for a tambourine.

In the kitchen of a hostel for women, on a Thursday, one of the residents comes in holding a letter and does not say anything for a moment. She is twenty-six and has been there nearly a year. The housing has come through. There are three other women in the room and one of them takes the letter off her, reads it, and reaches over to turn the radio up — the little one on the windowsill that is on all day and that nobody ever chooses. Two of them dance, badly, for about ninety seconds, holding on to each other and to the back of a chair, and then the kettle boils and somebody has to fetch their son from school. Nobody prayed and nobody said anything about God, and the radio carried on into whatever it was playing next.

That is not a lesser version of worship waiting to grow into the real thing. That is the reflex the Psalms were written to give words to, arriving before anybody had time to be self-conscious about it.

It has to be conceded that a station of continuous praise will get this wrong, and often. It will play a triumphant song into a room where nothing has been delivered — into the kitchen of somebody whose letter did not come, whose scan was bad, whose son has not rung. There is nothing gentle about a tambourine at the wrong moment. Anyone who has sat through a chorus about victory in the week of a funeral knows the particular loneliness of it.

But notice what Israel was actually singing on that bank. They had been slaves an hour earlier. Within three days they would be complaining bitterly about water, and the song did not stop being true when they did. A praise station is not a mood report and was never meant to be read as one — it is a fixed account of what God has done, kept sounding whether or not the room agrees with it this morning. This band carries frequencies for lament as well, and they matter. But the song after the sea is not waiting for your permission, and there are mornings when the best thing a radio can do is sing something you cannot yet mean.

So music is not the soft part of this ministry. It is the first response in the oldest account we have of God rescuing anybody, put onto a transmitter that does not stop. Deborah sings. David dances hard enough to embarrass his wife. Paul and Silas sing at midnight with their feet in the stocks, and the text bothers to mention that the other prisoners were listening — which is, more or less, radio.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Four kinds of programming sit on this dial, and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. Most of the band is music — praise and worship, contemporary, country, gospel, hymns and a good deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and explained and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to have on in a room with children in it, whether or not every track names God out loud. And there are the international frequencies, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. No menu, no queue to build, nothing to decide before anything starts.

If you want somewhere to begin, begin at HM 302.50 — Pentecostal Shout. It is the frequency on this band that behaves most like the bank of that sea: loud, bodily, unembarrassed, and entirely unbothered about whether you were ready. This article has argued that the first response to deliverance in Scripture was not a statement but a noise made with the whole person; that station is the nearest thing on the dial to hearing it done. Put it on while you are cooking or driving. You will notice within twenty minutes whether your objection is theological or simply that nobody has sung like that near you in a very long time.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play — it is built deliberately for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than an argument, because nobody on that bank had been argued into anything. Put HM 302.50 on this afternoon and let it run past the point where you would normally have turned it down. Something has happened to you at some stage — a sea closed behind you, whether or not you have ever put it that way. The tambourine has been waiting a long time to be picked up.
